claim: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are found across eukaryotes and can function in post-transcriptional gene regulation.
source: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are found across eukaryotes and can function in post-transcriptional gene regulation.
evidence: This is a general statement about circRNAs supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the broader literature.

claim: CircRNA biogenesis through a circle-forming backsplicing reaction is facilitated by reverse-complementary repetitive sequences promoting pre-mRNA folding.
source: Their biogenesis through a circle-forming backsplicing reaction is facilitated by reverse-complementary repetitive sequences promoting pre-mRNA folding.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field about circRNA biogenesis mechanisms.

claim: Orthologous genes from which circRNAs arise overall contain more strongly conserved splice sites and exons than other genes.
source: Orthologous genes from which circRNAs arise, overall contain more strongly conserved splice sites and exons than other genes, yet it remains unclear to what extent this conservation reflects purifying selection acting on the circRNAs themselves.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature and is presented as established knowledge.

claim: Surprisingly few circRNAs arise from orthologous exonic loci across all five species studied (opossum, mouse, rat, rhesus macaque, human).
source: Our analyses of circRNA repertoires from five species representing three mammalian lineages (marsupials, eutherians: rodents, primates) reveal that surprisingly few circRNAs arise from orthologous exonic loci across all species.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: CircRNAs from orthologous loci are associated with young, recently active and species-specific transposable elements.
source: Even the circRNAs from orthologous loci are associated with young, recently active and species-specific transposable elements, rather than with common, ancient transposon integration events.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of transposable elements in the manuscript.

claim: Many circRNAs emerged convergently during evolution as a byproduct of splicing in orthologs prone to transposon insertion.
source: These observations suggest that many circRNAs emerged convergently during evolution – as a byproduct of splicing in orthologs prone to transposon insertion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data analysis presented in the study.

claim: The findings argue against widespread functional circRNA conservation.
source: Overall, our findings argue against widespread functional circRNA conservation.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CircRNAs have gained significant prominence over the last decade.
source: First described more than 40 years ago, circular RNAs (circRNAs) were originally perceived as a curiosity of gene expression, yet they have gained significant prominence over the last decade (reviewed in Kristensen et al., 2019; Patop et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Large-scale sequencing efforts have led to the identification of thousands of individual circRNAs with specific expression patterns and, in some cases, specific functions.
source: Large-scale sequencing efforts have led to the identification of thousands of individual circRNAs with specific expression patterns and, in some cases, specific functions (Conn et al., 2015; Du et al., 2016; Hansen et al., 2013; Piwecka et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: CircRNA biogenesis involves backsplicing, in which an exon's 3' splice site is ligated onto an upstream 5' splice site of an exon on the same RNA molecule.
source: CircRNA biogenesis involves so-called 'backsplicing', in which an exon's 3' splice site is ligated onto an upstream 5' splice site of an exon on the same RNA molecule (rather than downstream, as in conventional splicing).
evidence: This is established knowledge about circRNA biogenesis.

claim: Backsplicing occurs co-transcriptionally and is guided by the canonical splicing machinery.
source: Backsplicing occurs co-transcriptionally and is guided by the canonical splicing machinery (Guo et al., 2014; Ashwal-Fluss et al., 2014; Starke et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Backsplicing can be facilitated by complementary, repetitive sequences in the flanking introns.
source: It can be facilitated by complementary, repetitive sequences in the flanking introns (Dubin et al., 1995; Jeck et al., 2013; Ashwal-Fluss et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014; Liang and Wilusz, 2014; Ivanov et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Intramolecular base-pairing and folding resulting in hairpin-like structures can augment backsplicing over the competing, regular forward-splicing reaction.
source: Through intramolecular base-pairing and folding, the resulting hairpin-like structures can augment backsplicing over the competing, regular forward-splicing reaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about RNA structure and splicing mechanisms.

claim: Backsplicing seems to be rather inefficient in most cases, as judged by the low circRNA expression levels found in many tissues.
source: Backsplicing seems to be rather inefficient in most cases, as judged by the low circRNA expression levels found in many tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed expression data.

claim: About 60% of circRNAs exhibit expression levels of less than 1 FPKM.
source: For example, it has been estimated that about 60% of circRNAs exhibit expression levels of less than 1 FPKM (fragments per kilobase per million reads mapped) – a commonly applied cut-off below which genes are usually considered to not be robustly expressed (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: CircRNAs are protected from the activity of cellular exonucleases due to their circular structure.
source: Due to their circular structure, circRNAs are protected from the activity of cellular exonucleases, which is thought to favour their accumulation to detectable steady-state levels and, together with the cell's proliferation history, presumably contributes to their complex spatiotemporal expression patterns (Alhasan et al., 2016; Memczak et al., 2013; Bachmayr-Heyda et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Overall higher circRNA abundances have been reported for neuronal tissues.
source: Overall higher circRNA abundances have been reported for neuronal tissues (Westholm et al., 2014; Gruner et al., 2016; Rybak-Wolf et al., 2015) and during ageing (Gruner et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2018; Cortés-López et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Higher circRNA abundances have been reported during ageing.
source: Overall higher circRNA abundances have been reported for neuronal tissues (Westholm et al., 2014; Gruner et al., 2016; Rybak-Wolf et al., 2015) and during ageing (Gruner et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2018; Cortés-López et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: All eukaryotes (protists, fungi, plants, animals) produce circRNAs.
source: All eukaryotes (protists, fungi, plants, animals) produce circRNAs (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: CircRNAs are frequently generated from orthologous genomic regions across species such as mouse, pig, and human.
source: Moreover, it has been reported that circRNAs are frequently generated from orthologous genomic regions across species such as mouse, pig, and human (Rybak-Wolf et al., 2015; Venø et al., 2015), and that their splice sites have elevated conservation scores (You et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: CircRNA splice sites have elevated conservation scores.
source: Moreover, it has been reported that circRNAs are frequently generated from orthologous genomic regions across species such as mouse, pig, and human (Rybak-Wolf et al., 2015; Venø et al., 2015), and that their splice sites have elevated conservation scores (You et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Previous analyses did not distinguish between potential selective constraints acting on the circRNAs themselves from those preserving canonical splicing features of parental genes.
source: However, the analyses did not distinguish between potential selective constraints actually acting on the circRNAs themselves, from those preserving canonical splicing features of genes in which they are formed (termed 'parental genes' in the following).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior studies based on inference.

claim: Long introns containing reverse complement sequences (RVCs) appear to be a conserved feature of circRNA parental genes.
source: Moreover, even though long introns containing reverse complement sequences (RVCs) appear to be a conserved feature of circRNA parental genes (Zhang et al., 2014; Rybak-Wolf et al., 2015), the rapid evolutionary changes occurring on the actual repeat sequences present a considerable obstacle to a thorough evolutionary understanding.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Concrete examples for experimentally validated, functionally conserved circRNAs are still rather scarce.
source: Finally, concrete examples for experimentally validated, functionally conserved circRNAs are still rather scarce.
evidence: This is an assessment based on knowledge of the literature.

claim: The difficulty to specifically target circular vs. linear transcript isoforms in loss-of-function experiments may explain the scarcity of functionally conserved circRNAs.
source: At least in part, the reason may lie in the difficulty to specifically target circular vs. linear transcript isoforms in loss-of-function experiments; only recently, novel dedicated tools for such experiments have been developed (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The prevalence of functional circRNA conservation remains overall unclear.
source: Currently, however, the prevalence of functional circRNA conservation remains overall unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The study generated a comprehensive set of circRNA-enriched RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data from five mammalian species and three organs.
source: Here, we set out to investigate the origins and evolution of circRNAs; to this end, we generated a comprehensive set of circRNA-enriched RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data from five mammalian species and three organs.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: CircRNAs are typically generated from a distinct class of genes that share characteristic structural and sequence features.
source: Our analyses unveil that circRNAs are typically generated from a distinct class of genes that share characteristic structural and sequence features.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: CircRNAs are flanked by species-specific and recently active transposable elements (TEs).
source: Notably, we discovered that circRNAs are flanked by species-specific and recently active transposable elements (TEs).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The integration of TEs is preferred in introns of genes with similar genomic properties, thus facilitating circRNA formation as a byproduct of splicing around the same exons of orthologous genes across different species.
source: Our findings support a model according to which the integration of TEs is preferred in introns of genes with similar genomic properties, thus facilitating circRNA formation as a byproduct of splicing around the same exons of orthologous genes across different species.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data analysis in the study.

claim: Most circRNAs may not trace back to common ancestral circRNAs but have rather emerged convergently during evolution, facilitated by independent TE insertion events.
source: Together, our work suggests that most circRNAs – even when occurring in orthologs of multiple species and comprising the same exons – may nevertheless not trace back to common ancestral circRNAs but have rather emerged convergently during evolution, facilitated by independent TE insertion events.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The study identified 1535 circRNAs in opossum, 1484 in mouse, 2038 in rat, 3300 in rhesus macaque, and 4491 circRNAs in human.
source: In total, following rigorous filtering, we identified 1535 circRNAs in opossum, 1484 in mouse, 2038 in rat, 3300 in rhesus macaque, and 4491 circRNAs in human, with overall higher numbers in cerebellum, followed by testis and liver (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript and Figure 1A.

claim: Overall higher numbers of circRNAs were detected in cerebellum, followed by testis and liver.
source: In total, following rigorous filtering, we identified 1535 circRNAs in opossum, 1484 in mouse, 2038 in rat, 3300 in rhesus macaque, and 4491 circRNAs in human, with overall higher numbers in cerebellum, followed by testis and liver (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript and Figure 1A.

claim: Identified circRNAs were generally small in size, overlapped with protein-coding exons, frequently detectable only in one of the tissues, and were flanked by long introns.
source: Identified circRNAs were generally small in size, overlapped with protein-coding exons, frequently detectable only in one of the tissues, and were flanked by long introns (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The number of hotspots and the number of individual circRNAs that they give rise to depend on the chosen CPM threshold.
source: As expected, the number of hotspots – and the number of individual circRNAs that they give rise to – depend on the chosen CPM threshold (Figure 1B for human and rhesus macaque data; Figure 1—figure supplement 4 for other species).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: At 0.1 CPM only 16–27% of all detected circRNA-generating loci are classified as hotspots.
source: Thus, at 0.1 CPM only 16–27% of all detected circRNA-generating loci are classified as hotspots.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Decreasing the stringency to 0.01 CPM increases the proportion of hotspot loci to 32–45%.
source: Decreasing the stringency to 0.01 CPM increases the proportion of hotspot loci to 32–45%.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The fraction of circRNAs that originate from hotspots increases from 34–49% (0.1 CPM) to 59–76% (0.01 CPM).
source: At the same time, the fraction of circRNAs that originate from hotspots (rather than from non-hotspot loci) increases from 34–49% (0.1 CPM) to 59–76% (0.01 CPM), and the number of circRNAs per hotspot increases from 2 to 6.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The number of circRNAs per hotspot increases from 2 to 6 when CPM threshold is lowered from 0.1 to 0.01.
source: At the same time, the fraction of circRNAs that originate from hotspots (rather than from non-hotspot loci) increases from 34–49% (0.1 CPM) to 59–76% (0.01 CPM), and the number of circRNAs per hotspot increases from 2 to 6.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: With lower CPM thresholds, the number of distinct circRNAs that become detectable per locus increases substantially.
source: Together, these analyses show that with lower CPM thresholds, the number of distinct circRNAs that become detectable per locus increases substantially; the number of detectable individual circRNA-generating loci increases as well, yet this effect is overall smaller.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: In many cases the same hotspots produce circRNAs across multiple organs.
source: Furthermore, we observed that in many cases the same hotspots produces circRNAs across multiple organs (Figure 1C), with typically one predominant circRNA expressed per organ (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript and Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Typically one predominant circRNA is expressed per organ from a hotspot.
source: Furthermore, we observed that in many cases the same hotspots produces circRNAs across multiple organs (Figure 1C), with typically one predominant circRNA expressed per organ (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript and Figure 1D.

claim: The Kansl1l hotspot locus produces six different circRNAs in rat.
source: The Kansl1l hotspot locus is a representative example: it is a hotspot in rat, where it produces six different circRNAs (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript and Figure 1E.

claim: The Kansl1l locus is a hotspot in all species studied and produces 8, 5, 7, and 6 different circRNAs in opossum, mouse, rhesus macaque and human, respectively.
source: It is also a hotspot in all other species and produces 8, 5, 7, and 6 different circRNAs in opossum, mouse, rhesus macaque and human, respectively (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The expression levels of many circRNAs are low.
source: Overall, we concluded that the expression levels of many circRNAs are low.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Increasing the sensitivity of detection (i.e. lowering CPM thresholds) led to a substantial gain in the detectability of additional, low-expressed circRNA species, but less so of additional circRNA-generating genomic loci.
source: Increasing the sensitivity of detection (i.e. lowering CPM thresholds) led to a substantial gain in the detectability of additional, low-expressed circRNA species, but less so of additional circRNA-generating genomic loci.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many of the circRNAs that can be identified may reflect a form of gene expression noise that occurred preferentially at hotspot loci, rather than functional transcriptome diversity.
source: These findings raised the question whether many of the circRNAs that can be identified reflected a form of gene expression noise that occurred preferentially at hotspot loci, rather than functional transcriptome diversity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data analysis.

claim: The study annotated 5428 circRNA loci across all species.
source: In total, we annotated 5428 circRNA loci across all species (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript and Figure 2A.

claim: The majority of circRNA loci are species-specific (4103 loci; corresponding to 75.6% of all annotated loci).
source: The majority of loci are species-specific (4103 loci; corresponding to 75.6% of all annotated loci); there are only comparatively few instances where circRNAs arise from orthologous loci in the different species (i.e. from loci that share orthologous exons in corresponding 1:1 orthologous genes; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript and Figure 2A.

claim: Only 260 orthologous loci (4.8% of all loci) give rise to circRNAs in all five species.
source: For example, only 260 orthologous loci (4.8% of all loci) give rise to circRNAs in all five species (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript and Figure 2A.

claim: A considerable proportion of shared loci also correspond to circRNA hotspots (opossum: 28.0%, mouse: 43.6%, rat: 53.0%, rhesus macaque: 46.2%, human: 61.6%).
source: A considerable proportion of these shared loci also correspond to circRNA hotspots (opossum: 28.0%, mouse: 43.6%, rat: 53.0%, rhesus macaque: 46.2%, human: 61.6%; calculated from hotspot counts in Figure 1B and loci counts in Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and figures.

claim: Despite applying circRNA enrichment strategies for library preparation and lenient thresholds for computational identification, the number of potentially conserved orthologous circRNAs is surprisingly low.
source: Thus, despite applying circRNA enrichment strategies for library preparation and lenient thresholds for computational identification, the number of potentially conserved orthologous circRNAs is surprisingly low.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The use of additional evolutionary species drove the strong reduction in potentially conserved circRNA candidates.
source: Further analyses confirmed that also in our datasets, it was the use of additional evolutionary species that drove the strong reduction in potentially conserved circRNA candidates – see for example how the addition of the rat or of rhesus macaque datasets affect the human-mouse comparison (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CircRNA exons showed higher phastCons scores than exons from the same genes that were not spliced into circRNAs.
source: CircRNA exons showed higher phastCons scores than exons from the same genes that were not spliced into circRNAs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 2B.

claim: 85–95% of the observed median differences in phastCons scores between circRNA exons and non-parental genes could be explained by the parental gene itself.
source: First, the comparison of phastCons scores between exons of non-parental genes, parental genes and circRNAs revealed that parental genes were per se highly conserved (Figure 2B): 85–95% of the observed median differences between circRNA exons and non-parental genes could be explained by the parental gene itself.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 2B.

claim: CircRNA exons are more frequently used in isoforms expressed in multiple organs than non-circRNA parental gene exons.
source: Next, we compared the usage of parental gene exons across organs (Figure 2C). We observed that circRNA exons are more frequently used in isoforms expressed in multiple organs than non-circRNA parental gene exons.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 2C.

claim: GC amplitudes are significantly higher for circRNA-internal exons than for parental gene exons that were located outside of circRNAs.
source: Finally, we analysed the sequence composition at the splice sites, which revealed that GC amplitudes (i.e. the differences in GC content at the intron-exon boundary) are significantly higher for circRNA-internal exons than for parental gene exons that were located outside of circRNAs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 2D.

claim: The supposed high conservation of circRNAs may not be directly associated with the circRNAs themselves, but with constitutive exons that the circRNAs contain.
source: Collectively, these observations (i.e. increased phastCons scores, expression in multiple tissues, increased GC amplitudes) prompt the question whether the exon properties associated with circRNAs actually reflect at their core an enrichment for constitutive exons. Under this scenario, the supposed high conservation of circRNAs may not be directly associated with the circRNAs themselves, but with constitutive exons that the circRNAs contain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many of the circRNAs 'shared' across species might actually not be homologous but may have emerged independently (convergently) during evolution.
source: Thus, even many of the circRNAs 'shared' across species might actually not be homologous. That is, rather than reflecting (divergent) evolution from common ancestral circRNAs (Figure 2E, left panel), they may frequently have emerged independently (convergently) during evolution in the lineages leading to the different species, thus potentially representing 'analogous' transcriptional traits (Figure 2E, right panel).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 2E.

claim: The increased GC amplitudes at circRNA exon-intron boundaries were mainly caused by a local decrease of intronic GC content rather than by an increase in exonic GC content.
source: We realised that the increased GC amplitudes at circRNA exon-intron boundaries (see above, Figure 2D) were mainly caused by a local decrease of intronic GC content rather than by an increase in exonic GC content (Supplementary file 5, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and supplementary materials.

claim: Non-parental genes displayed a unimodal distribution in the two rodents (peak in H1), were generally GC-poor in opossum (peak in L1), and showed a more complex isochore structure in rhesus macaque and human (peaks in L2 and H3).
source: Non-parental genes displayed a unimodal distribution in the two rodents (peak in H1), were generally GC-poor in opossum (peak in L1), and showed a more complex isochore structure in rhesus macaque and human (peaks in L2 and H3), in agreement with previous findings (Galtier and Mouchiroud, 1998; Mikkelsen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: CircRNA parental genes showed a distinctly different distribution than non-parental genes and a consistent pattern across all five species, with the majority of genes (82–94% depending on species) distributing to the GC-low gene groups, L1 and L2.
source: Notably, circRNA parental genes showed a distinctly different distribution than non-parental genes and a consistent pattern across all five species, with the majority of genes (82–94% depending on species) distributing to the GC-low gene groups, L1 and L2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 3A.

claim: Parental genes showed more pronounced self-complementarity than non-parental genes within the same GC isochore.
source: This analysis revealed more pronounced self-complementarity for parental genes than for non-parental genes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 3B.

claim: CircRNA parental genes are biased towards early replicating genes, showed higher steady-state expression levels, and are characterised by increased haploinsufficiency scores.
source: Using data from three human cell studies (Steinberg et al., 2015; Pai et al., 2012; Koren et al., 2012), our analyses revealed that circRNA parental genes are biased towards early replicating genes, showed higher steady-state expression levels, and are characterised by increased haploinsufficiency scores (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: CircRNA parental genes exhibit distinct structural features (low GC content, high repetitiveness) and specific functional properties associated with important roles in human cells.
source: Collectively, we conclude that circRNA parental genes exhibit not only distinct structural features (low GC content, high repetitiveness), but also specific functional properties associated with important roles in human cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Predictions of circRNA parental genes occurred with high precision (accuracy 72–79%, sensitivity of 75%, specificity 71–79% across all species).
source: Notably, predictions occurred with high precision (accuracy 72–79%, sensitivity of 75%, specificity 71–79% across all species) and uncovered several significantly associated features (Table 1, Supplementary file 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript, Table 1, and supplementary materials.

claim: The main parental gene predictors are low GC content (log-odds ratio -1.84 to -0.72) and increased number of exons in the gene (log-odds ratio 0.30 to 0.45).
source: Consistently for all species, the main parental gene predictors are low GC content (log-odds ratio -1.84 to -0.72) and increased number of exons in the gene (log-odds ratio 0.30 to 0.45).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Features positively associated with circRNA production are increased genomic length (log-odds ratio 0.17 to 0.26), increased proportion of reverse-complementary areas (repeat fragments) within the gene (log-odds ratio 0.20 to 0.59), increased expression levels (log-odds ratio 0.25 to 0.38) and higher phastCons scores (log-odds ratio 0.45 to 0.58).
source: Furthermore, features positively associated with circRNA production are increased genomic length (log-odds ratio 0.17 to 0.26), increased proportion of reverse-complementary areas (repeat fragments) within the gene (log-odds ratio 0.20 to 0.59), increased expression levels (log-odds ratio 0.25 to 0.38) and higher phastCons scores (log-odds ratio 0.45 to 0.58) (Table 1, Figure 3C–D, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript, Table 1, Figure 3C-D, and supplementary materials.

claim: Parental genes of previously reported functional human circRNAs obtain high prediction values in the model and share specific properties.
source: Notably, parental genes of previously reported functional human circRNAs – for example, circHipk3 (Zheng et al., 2016) and circMbnl1 (Ashwal-Fluss et al., 2014) that sequester miRNAs and proteins, respectively – obtain high prediction values in our model and share the above specific properties (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 3—figure supplement 3, supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The identified circRNA parental gene predictors were not restricted to the study's datasets but could be determined from independent circRNA data as well.
source: In addition, the identified circRNA parental gene predictors were not restricted to our datasets but could be determined from independent circRNA data as well.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis of independent datasets presented in the manuscript.

claim: The analysis of mouse and human heart tissue data revealed that circRNA parental genes were low in GC content, exon-rich, and showed enrichment for repeats.
source: Thus, the analysis of mouse and human heart tissue data (Werfel et al., 2016) – on which our linear regression models predicted parental genes with comparable accuracy (74%), sensitivity (75%), and specificity (74%) – revealed that circRNA parental genes were low in GC content, exon-rich, and showed enrichment for repeats (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis of independent datasets presented in the manuscript and Figure 3—figure supplement 4, supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The identified properties likely represent generic characteristics of circRNA parental genes that are suitable to distinguish them from non-parental genes.
source: In conclusion, the identified properties likely represent generic characteristics of circRNA parental genes that are suitable to distinguish them from non-parental genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: TEs belonging to the class of Short Interspersed Nuclear Elements (SINEs) are enriched within the circRNA flanking introns as compared to the control introns in all species.
source: In all species, TEs belonging to the class of Short Interspersed Nuclear Elements (SINEs) are enriched within the circRNA flanking introns as compared to the control introns.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The resulting TE enrichment profiles were exquisitely lineage-specific, and even largely species-specific.
source: Remarkably, the resulting TE enrichment profiles were exquisitely lineage-specific, and even largely species-specific (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 4A.

claim: In mouse, the order of enrichment is from the B1 class of rodent-specific B elements (strongest enrichment and highest frequency of >7.5 TEs per flanking intron) to B2 and B4 SINEs.
source: In mouse, for instance, the order of enrichment is from the B1 class of rodent-specific B elements (strongest enrichment and highest frequency of >7.5 TEs per flanking intron) to B2 and B4 SINEs.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: In rat, B1 (strong enrichment, yet less frequent than in mouse) is followed by ID (Identifier) elements, which are a family of small TEs characterised by a recent, strong amplification history in the rat lineage.
source: In rat, B1 (strong enrichment, yet less frequent than in mouse) is followed by ID (Identifier) elements, which are a family of small TEs characterised by a recent, strong amplification history in the rat lineage (Kim et al., 1994; Kim and Deininger, 1996); B2 and B4 SINEs only followed in 3rd and 4th position.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In rhesus macaque and human, Alu elements are the most frequent and strongly enriched TEs (around 14 TEs per intron), consistent with the known strong amplification history in the common primate ancestor.
source: In rhesus macaque and human, Alu elements are the most frequent and strongly enriched TEs (around 14 TEs per intron), consistent with the known strong amplification history in the common primate ancestor (reviewed in Batzer and Deininger, 2002; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 4A, and is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Relatively few specific dimers represented the majority of all predicted dimers (i.e. top-5 dimers accounted for 78% of all dimers in flanking introns in opossum, and for 50%, 55%, 43%, and 38% in mouse, rat, rhesus macaque and human, respectively).
source: Our analyses revealed that relatively few specific dimers represented the majority of all predicted dimers (i.e. top-5 dimers accounted for 78% of all dimers in flanking introns in opossum, and for 50%, 55%, 43%, and 38% in mouse, rat, rhesus macaque and human, respectively) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 4B.

claim: The most frequently occurring dimers (top-5 dimers) are formed by recently active TE family members.
source: Importantly, this analysis suggests that the most frequently occurring dimers (top-5 dimers are depicted with blue connecting lines in Figure 4F) are formed by recently active TE family members.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 4F.

claim: In mouse, the dimers formed by the B1_Mm, B1_Mus1, and B1_Mus2 elements are among the most recent (and still active) TEs in this species.
source: In mouse, an illustrative example are the dimers formed by the B1_Mm, B1_Mus1, and B1_Mus2 elements (Figure 4F), which are among the most recent (and still active) TEs in this species (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 4C and 4F.

claim: The dominant dimers in rat were the recently amplified ID elements, and not the more abundant (yet older in their amplification history) B1 family of TEs.
source: For example, the dominant dimers in rat were the recently amplified ID elements, and not the more abundant (yet older in their amplification history) B1 family of TEs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B; Kim et al., 1994; Kim and Deininger, 1996).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, and is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In opossum, the most prominent dimers consisted of opossum-specific SINE1 elements, which are similar to the Alu elements in primates, but possess an independent origin.
source: In opossum, the most prominent dimers consisted of opossum-specific SINE1 elements, which are similar to the Alu elements in primates, but possess an independent origin (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A; Gu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, and is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Within the primate lineage, the dimer composition was more uniform, probably due to the high amplification rate of the AluS subfamily (>650000 copies) in the common ancestor of Old World monkeys and the relatively recent divergence time of macaque and human.
source: Finally, within the primate lineage, the dimer composition was more uniform, probably due to the high amplification rate of the AluS subfamily (>650000 copies) in the common ancestor of Old World monkeys and the relatively recent divergence time of macaque and human (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–D; Deininger, 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C-D, and is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Dimer-forming sequences in circRNA flanking introns were most frequently composed of recent, and often currently still active, TEs.
source: In conclusion, the above analyses of RVCs revealed that dimer-forming sequences in circRNA flanking introns were most frequently composed of recent, and often currently still active, TEs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The dimer repertoires were specific to the lineages (marsupials, rodents, primates) and/or species-specific.
source: Therefore, the dimer repertoires were specific to the lineages (marsupials, rodents, primates) and/or (as most clearly visible within the rodent lineage) even species-specific.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The most frequent dimers are consistently formed by the youngest elements in both groups of genes (shared and species-specific).
source: The analysis revealed that the most frequent dimers are consistently formed by the youngest elements in both groups of genes, and that the frequency distribution of the top-100 dimers was significantly different between species (see Figure 5A for rat and human; other species in Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In rat, all top-5 dimers are composed of repeats from the youngest ID family members.
source: In rat, for instance, all top-5 dimers are composed of repeats from the youngest ID family members; in human, dimers involving AluY elements are strongly enriched (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 5A.

claim: In human, dimers involving AluY elements are strongly enriched.
source: In rat, for instance, all top-5 dimers are composed of repeats from the youngest ID family members; in human, dimers involving AluY elements are strongly enriched (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 5A.

claim: On average, most dimers occur at least once or twice per shared circRNA gene, corresponding to a 1.4- to 2.1-fold enrichment in comparison to species-specific circRNA loci.
source: On average, most dimers occur at least once or twice per shared circRNA gene, corresponding to a 1.4- to 2.1-fold enrichment in comparison to species-specific circRNA loci (Supplementary file 11).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and supplementary materials.

claim: Although Akt3 circRNAs are shared between human, mouse, and opossum, the dimer landscapes are entirely species-specific.
source: A representative example for a shared circRNA-generating locus with its complex dimer interaction landscape, involving young species-specific repeats, is the Akt3 locus (Figure 5B). Thus, although Akt3 circRNAs are shared between human (upper panel), mouse (middle panel), and opossum (lower panel), the dimer landscapes are entirely specifies-specific (see top-5 dimers that are highlighted in the figure).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 5B.

claim: There were no significant differences in milliDiv values between species-specific and shared parental genes in any of the species.
source: Following this rationale, we determined in each species the degradation rates for the repeats forming the top-5 dimers. Comparing their milliDiv values species-specific parental genes revealed no significant differences in any of the species (Figure 5C – left panel, Figure 5—figure supplement 3 – left panel).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: No difference in minimal free energies (MFEs) of dimer formation was detected between shared and species-specific groups, suggesting that dimers of shared circRNA loci are not subject to a specific selection pressure.
source: To this end, we selected the least-degraded dimer for every parental gene in both groups (shared/species-specific) and calculated the minimal free energies (MFEs) of dimer formation. We detected no difference between the groups, suggesting that dimers of shared circRNA loci are not subject to a specific selection pressure, but degrade identically to dimers in species-specific circRNA loci (Figure 5C – right panel, Figure 5—figure supplement 3 – right panel).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Dimers comprising 'intermediate age' repeats could be found in the species-specific 'least-degraded' dimers, yet they were absent from the shared group, which rather contained the top-1/top-2 most enriched and youngest dimers.
source: Furthermore, we observed that dimers comprising 'intermediate age' repeats (i.e. B1_Mur2, B1_Mur3, B1_Mur4, present in Muridae) could be found in the species-specific 'least-degraded' dimers, yet they were absent from the shared group, which rather contained the top-1/top-2 most enriched and youngest dimers (e.g. AluSx+AluY and AluSx1+AluY in human Figure 5C; ID_Rn1+ID_Rn1 and ID_Rn1+ID_Rn2 in rat) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: CircRNAs are preferentially formed from loci that have attracted transposons in recent evolutionary history.
source: Taken together, we conclude that circRNAs are preferentially formed from loci that have attracted transposons in recent evolutionary history.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Even in the case of shared circRNA loci the actual repeat landscapes, dimer predictions, transposon ages and degradation rates, as well as RVC pairing energies, are most consistent with the model that circRNAs are analogous features that have been formed by convergent evolution.
source: Even in the case of shared circRNA loci the actual repeat landscapes, dimer predictions, transposon ages and degradation rates, as well as RVC pairing energies, are most consistent with the model that circRNAs are analogous features that have been formed by convergent evolution, rather than homologous features originating from a common circRNA ancestor.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Many circRNAs have not evolved from common, ancestral circRNA loci, but have emerged independently through convergent evolution, most likely driven by structural commonalities of their parental genes.
source: In our study, we have investigated this topic through the analysis of novel, dedicated cross-species datasets. Notably, we propose that many circRNAs have not evolved from common, ancestral circRNA loci, but have emerged independently through convergent evolution, most likely driven by structural commonalities of their parental genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Genetic loci giving rise to circRNAs are generally long, exon-rich and located in genomic regions of low GC content.
source: Thus, the modelling of parental genes uncovered features that are associated with circRNA biogenesis, in support of the concept of a 'circRNA niche' in which circRNAs are more likely to be generated: genetic loci giving rise to circRNAs are generally long, exon-rich and located in genomic regions of low GC content.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the case of orthologous parental genes, structural characteristics are shared, and they have led to shared integration biases for transposons, that is to shared, genomic 'TE hotspots'.
source: In the case of orthologous parental genes, these structural characteristics are shared as well, and they have led to shared integration biases for transposons, that is to shared, genomic 'TE hotspots'.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Because the actual TEs predicted as most relevant for dimerisation are mostly not shared across species and are evolutionarily young, the resulting circRNAs are evolutionarily young as well.
source: Thus, because the actual TEs predicted as most relevant for dimerisation are mostly not shared across species and are evolutionarily young, we propose that the resulting circRNAs are evolutionarily young as well.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: CircRNAs from orthologous genes frequently do not involve exactly the same 5' and 3' backsplice sites and thus do not encompass precisely the same orthologous exons, but show partial exon overlap across species.
source: In line with this interpretation, circRNAs from orthologous genes frequently do not involve exactly the same 5' and 3' backsplice sites and thus do not encompass precisely the same orthologous exons, but show partial exon overlap across species (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The model provides an explanation for how circRNAs can arise from orthologous exonic loci across species even if they themselves are not homologous.
source: Our model provides an explanation for how circRNAs can arise from orthologous exonic loci across species even if they themselves are not homologous (i.e. they do not stem from common evolutionary precursors that emerged in common ancestors).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model proposed in the manuscript.

claim: If most circRNAs are evolutionarily young, then, by extension, it is overall rather unlikely that they fulfil crucial functions.
source: Importantly, if most circRNAs are evolutionarily young, then, by extension, it is overall rather unlikely that they fulfil crucial functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conclusions of the study.

claim: The idea that most circRNAs are unlikely to fulfil crucial functions is in agreement with the generally low expression levels of circRNAs that have been reported and with accumulation patterns that are frequently tissue-specific and confined to post-mitotic cells.
source: This idea is in agreement with the generally low expression levels of circRNAs that have been reported and with accumulation patterns that are frequently tissue-specific and confined to post-mitotic cells (Guo et al., 2014; Westholm et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The main conclusions of this study overlap with those of two independent manuscripts that have appeared in press and as a publication preprint.
source: Importantly, these and other main conclusions of our study overlap with those of two independent manuscripts (with complementary data and analyses) that have appeared in press (Xu and Zhang, 2021) and as a publication preprint (Santos-Rodriguez et al., 2021), respectively, while we were preparing the revised version of our manuscript.
evidence: This is a statement about the convergence of findings with other studies, supported by citations.

claim: TE integration close to a very strong splice site with a strong GC amplitude would have lower impact and would be tolerated better than integration close to alternative exons.
source: By contrast, TE integration close to a very strong splice site with a strong GC amplitude – as typically found in canonical exons – would have lower impact. Hence, it would be tolerated better than integration close to alternative exons, whose GC amplitudes are less pronounced.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of splicing mechanisms and the data presented.

claim: CircRNA exons are typically canonical exons with strong GC amplitudes.
source: Indeed, our analyses show that circRNA exons are typically canonical exons with strong GC amplitudes.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The increased phastCons scores of circRNA exons are a mere consequence of a higher tolerance for TE integration in introns flanking canonical exons.
source: While at first sight, circRNA exons thus appear to be endowed with rather specific, evolutionarily relevant properties – most notably with increased phastCons scores – it is probable that these are a mere consequence of a higher tolerance for TE integration in introns flanking canonical exons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis and model proposed in the manuscript.

claim: The probability that a TE integration event is tolerated will be overall lower in short and compact genes as compared to genes with long introns.
source: Thus, the probability that an integration event is tolerated, will be overall lower in short and compact genes as compared to genes with long introns; of note, long genes are also GC-poor (Zhu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: CircRNAs are frequently generated from GC-poor genes with long introns, complex gene structures, and that contain many TEs.
source: These characteristics overlap precisely with those that we identify for circRNAs, which are also frequently generated from GC-poor genes with long introns, complex gene structures, and that contain many TEs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Associations between RNA editing and circRNA abundances are likely a secondary effect from the primary purpose of A-to-I editing, namely the inhibition of Alu amplification.
source: However, A-to-I editing is also a well-known defense mechanism that has evolved to suppress TE amplification. For example, A-to-I RNA editing is associated with intronic Alu elements to inhibit Alu dimers (Lev-Maor et al., 2008; Athanasiadis et al., 2004). Therefore, it is quite likely that associations between RNA editing and circRNA abundances are a secondary effect from the primary purpose of A-to-I editing, namely the inhibition of Alu amplification.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The link of circRNAs to m6A may simply reflect the general targeting of erroneous transcripts for degradation.
source: Or, in the case of N6-methyladenosine (m6A), it has recently been proposed that this highly prevalent RNA modification is also involved in dynamically regulating circRNA abundances (Zhou et al., 2017; Park et al., 2019; Di Timoteo et al., 2020). Yet the link of circRNAs to m6A, which is known to influence many steps of mRNA metabolism (reviewed in Zaccara et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2020), may simply reflect the general targeting of erroneous transcripts for degradation.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Many circRNAs are likely a form of transcript noise – or, more precisely, of mis-splicing – that is provoked by TE integration into parental genes.
source: In summary, our evolutionary data and the above considerations lead us to conclude that many circRNAs are likely a form of transcript noise – or, more precisely, of mis-splicing – that is provoked by TE integration into parental genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis and inference presented in the manuscript.

claim: This conclusion is in full agreement with the observation that in rat neurons, there is a direct correspondence between the pharmacological inhibition of canonical splicing and increased circRNA formation, preferentially affecting circRNAs with long introns and many transposons/RVCs.
source: This conclusion is in full agreement with the observation that in rat neurons, there is a direct correspondence between the pharmacological inhibition of canonical splicing and increased circRNA formation, preferentially affecting circRNAs with long introns and many transposons/RVCs (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The majority of circRNAs do not have specific molecular functions, although functional circRNAs have arisen during evolution.
source: Altogether, these conclusions make it likely that the majority of circRNAs do not have specific molecular functions, although functional circRNAs have arisen during evolution, as demonstrated in several studies (e.g. Hansen et al., 2013; Conn et al., 2015; Du et al., 2016), presumably from initially non-functional (noise) variants whose emergence was facilitated by the aforementioned mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on data analysis and inference, supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A functional circRNA may ultimately become independent from the original RVC-based regulation by evolving from a sequence-based backsplice mechanism to a protein-based one.
source: During this process, a functional circRNA may ultimately even become independent from the original RVC-based regulation. Evolving from a sequence-based backsplice mechanism to a protein-based one (i.e. relying on RNA-binding proteins, RBPs) could render regulation more versatile and more controllable.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolution of functional circRNAs.

claim: RBPs have emerged as important regulators of several circRNAs.
source: Indeed, RBPs have emerged as important regulators of several circRNAs (see e.g. Ashwal-Fluss et al., 2014; Conn et al., 2015; Okholm et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The functions of circRNAs seem to be diverse and may often involve the positive or negative regulation of their own parental genes at different expression layers through various mechanisms.
source: The functions of circRNAs seem to be diverse and may often involve the positive or negative regulation of their own parental genes at different expression layers (transcription/splicing, translation, post-translational modification) through various mechanisms (e.g. competition with linear mRNA splicing, microRNA sponge effects, mRNA traps) (Shao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: CircRNAs have emerged as reliable disease biomarkers.
source: Finally, we would like to note that circRNAs have emerged as reliable disease biomarkers (Memczak et al., 2015; Bahn et al., 2015), and their utility for such predictive purposes is not diminished by our conclusion that most circRNAs are unlikely to fulfil direct functions – on the contrary.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: An altered circRNA profile could hint at misregulated transcription or splicing of the parental gene, at a novel TE integration event, or at problems with RNA editing or methylation machineries.
source: Even if an altered circRNA profile will likely not indicate causal involvement in a disease, it could hint at misregulated transcription or splicing of the parental gene, at a novel TE integration event, or at problems with RNA editing or methylation machineries.
evidence: This is an inference about the potential utility of circRNAs as biomarkers.
